results.evidence: No statute numbers appear anywhere in the post; all legal rules are described with general language like 'in most jurisdictions' and 'the legal limit'.

No individual attorney or legal-scholar names appear; citations reference organizations (Innocence Project, NHTSA) and journals (Forensic Science International, Journal of Analytical Toxicology) only.

All statistics are sourced: ±0.005–0.02 BAC margin (Forensic Science International), 375+ exonerations (Innocence Project), 1100:1–3500:1 partition ratio range (Journal of Analytical Toxicology), NHTSA Conforming Products List cited in TLDR.

Every procedural claim is jurisdiction-qualified: calibration 'every 30, 60, or 90 days depending on the model and jurisdiction,' observation period '15 to 20 minutes (varies by jurisdiction),' partition ratio '2100:1 in most jurisdictions.'
No case citations appear; the Innocence Project is referenced as an organization, not a case name.
No specific collateral-consequence claims appear; the post focuses on challenging breath test evidence, not on sentencing or post-conviction consequences.

results.reason: Frontmatter has no question_count field to validate against; body contains 2 explicit quoted attorney questions plus several implied 'ask your attorney' prompts
Key claims are sourced (Forensic Science International for margin of error, Innocence Project for 375+ exonerations, Journal of Analytical Toxicology for partition ratios, NHTSA for device list)
Action items use plain direct language ('Ask your attorney...', 'Write down...', 'Count back 30 days') accessible at or below 10th grade level
None of the flagged cliches ('end of the day', 'tip of the iceberg', 'slippery slope', 'double-edged sword', 'game changer', 'wake-up call') appear in the post
Consistent second-person 'you/your' throughout; third-person references are only to external actors (officer, prosecution, attorney), never to the reader
Passive constructions appear occasionally ('is supposed to be observed', 'was calibrated') but well under the 30% threshold; most sentences are active

'Hematocrit' is used without definition and 'discovery request' appears multiple times without a first-use definition, though most legal terms (partition ratio, calibration, suppression motions) are contextualized
Logical flow: hook → problem framing → four numbered challenge points → consolidated discovery list → closing empowerment; no orphaned paragraphs
Multiple clear next steps: specific attorney question to quote, Case Progress Score link, DUI Defense Playbook link, and a numbered discovery list to email the attorney
Action statements are direct ('Ask your attorney', 'Write down', 'Count back 30 days'); hedges like 'could' and 'may' appear mainly in information statements about outcomes, which is allowed
All paragraphs are well under 300 words and action paragraphs stay under 100 words; the longest observation-period paragraph is broken into digestible blocks
The four challenge-point sections plus intro, discovery list, and closing are roughly balanced; no single section approaches 50% of total word count

Every threat (wrong BAC, .08 could be .10, uncertified operator, overdue calibration) is paired with a specific action within 1-2 sentences (ask the question, write it down, email the list, check the timestamps)

Strong hook ('The number isn't a fact. It's an opinion from a machine.'), evidence-driven middle with four concrete challenge points and sourced claims, empowering close with specific 5-minute actions

results.evidence: Post frames actions as questions to ask attorney ('Ask your attorney whether they've reviewed the bodycam footage') rather than directives to the reader.
Every challenge section ends with attorney redirect like 'Ask your attorney whether they've confirmed the operator's certification' and 'five-minute conversation with your attorney.'
Post discusses margin of error generally ('a reading of .08 could actually be anywhere from .06 to .10') without evaluating the specific reader's case strength.

Post states 'your attorney should be using these gaps to file suppression motions' and 'that's a challenge your attorney needs to file — today, not next month' — recommending specific motions be filed.
Post does not discuss immigration consequences at all, so no immigration-specific redirect is required.
Collateral consequences are not discussed; technical claims are sourced to NHTSA, Forensic Science International, Journal of Analytical Toxicology, and Innocence Project.
Device models (Intoxilyzer 8000, Alco-Sensor FST, Draeger 9510) are named only as examples of different machines, not as recommendations of companies or firms.
Post does not use 'we recommend' or similar phrasing in legal-action contexts; 'What We Do' section describes services not legal recommendations.
Hypothetical framings like 'You're standing in a police station' and 'The officer arrests you' are written in second-person scene-setting, clearly illustrative rather than claims about a real case.
Post consistently frames knowledge as 'questions to bring to your attorney' and 'ask your attorney' rather than enabling self-representation.
Post uses qualifiers like 'typically every 30, 60, or 90 days depending on the model and jurisdiction' and '(varies by jurisdiction)' when stating rules.

Post states 'This is one of the strongest foundations for getting a DUI case dismissed' and 'Five minutes of preparation unlocks months of defense' — implying specific outcomes without qualification that results vary.

Strategies are attributed to the Innocence Project methodology, NHTSA, Forensic Science International, and Journal of Analytical Toxicology rather than presented as the blog's original legal positions.
No contradictory legal claims appear; calibration cycles, margin of error ranges, and observation period lengths are consistently qualified.
Products framed as research tools: 'analyze DUI cases and identify exactly which records your attorney should be pulling' and 'give you the questions to bring to your attorney.'

Opening reframes the BAC number but doesn't name fear until sentence 4 ('Your BAC result feels like a verdict'); several H2s like 'The Machine Has a History' and 'The It's Just a Number Problem' are topical rather than action-oriented
'Discovery requests', 'suppression motions', and 'hematocrit levels' appear without inline definitions on first use; paragraphs are otherwise short and partition ratio is defined inline

Pre-H2 content ends with 'its value depends entirely on how it was collected' — no immediate-action block before the first H2; first concrete action ('Ask your attorney one question today') is buried in the middle of section 1
Each challenge point leads with a single clear default action (request calibration records, verify certification, check observation period against bodycam timestamps)
The 'What Your Attorney Should Be Requesting' section contains a 7-item numbered discovery list with no 'start with these' priority grouping, exceeding the 5-item unranked ceiling
Structural pattern: system-decoder-post — decodes the breathalyzer evidence system into four challenge points

Margin-of-error threat is followed by 'worth a five-minute conversation with your attorney'; overdue calibration threat is followed by 'Look up your arrest date. Count back 30 days'; each fear is paired with a specific action within 2 sentences
No 'you should have' or 'if you had' patterns — blame is directed at the machine, department procedures, and attorneys who don't request records, never at the reader

Arc is present (fear reframe → process explanation → agency closers like 'Five minutes of preparation unlocks months of defense') but the actual final sentence before the disclaimer is a generic CTA to the Case Progress Score and playbook
No tables, only H2 heading level used, key actions bolded as screenshot sentences, and each challenge section stays in the 400-500 word range

Every H2 section has a bolded sentence but 'A breathalyzer overdue for calibration...' (28 words), 'A .08 reading with a ±0.02 margin...' (28 words), and 'If the prosecution can't produce complete...' (30 words) exceed the 27-word ceiling
All three FAQ answers start with the direct answer, stay within 2-4 sentences, and read as insider observations rather than institutional policy explanations
